validated_work_order.understanding:
#71's PR (#73) merged with seven review findings and one QA finding open; this ticket is the lot, and v1 of this work order was rejected on one blocking finding about the width condition, which the proposal has now measured and corrected.

I re-read both documents and the code. The diagnosis is right and I confirmed the load-bearing parts myself: src/web/styles.css is read in eight places in test/web/pages.test.js (lines 345, 359, 1633, 1653, 1693, 1757, 1802, 1819) and each builds its own parser; the min-width pin's regex is /^(ch|rem|px)$/ compared as a bare number, so min-width: 12px is green today; the min-width, #main:focus and .page-title pins all parse raw bodies and are comment-blind; the card pin's parse cannot see inside an at-rule; and .awaiting-list is display: grid with a .awaiting-list li carrying no overflow-wrap. I ran the baseline myself: node --test test/web/pages.test.js reads 72 tests / 71 pass / 1 fail, the failure being the /<li class="approval-card">/ matcher. The 8-or-5 scope question, the at-rule blind spot and the unit false green are all real.

The proposal's correction of v1's blocking rejection is right and I checked its reasoning: document.documentElement.scrollWidth is the content box and window.innerWidth includes the scrollbar, so a page with no horizontal overflow at all reads scrollWidth 305 against innerWidth 320 on this runner. AC-1 and qa_script step 4 are restated as scrollWidth === clientWidth, with 305/360/399 as the expected values and the 15px classic scrollbar named. That is the fix, not a dodge. AC-2 is left alone as the reviewer directed, and it is already consistent.

What I changed as arbiter, and why, is in debate_summary; the four that matter are structural rather than cosmetic. (1) The shared laterOverrides helper must be property-filtered. The card pin filters its candidate rules on /overflow-wrap\s*:/ today, and that filter is what makes the unrelated-rule tolerance #71 added deliberately work; a helper that takes only a selector set either drops that tolerance or hardcodes the property, and both break something this order promises. (2) AC-10's element sweep must run against clientWidth, not innerWidth — an innerWidth threshold is structurally blind to any overflow up to a scrollbar wide, and the proposal's own recorded 4px on /approvals is the proof. (3) The /approvals 4px is diagnosed and named as a pre-existing offender rather than left as a guess; I confirmed the CSS shape that makes it what the critic says it is, and it is not fixed here. (4) AC-5 is restated as a delta plus a test name, because tests[] and a criterion that pins exact totals cannot both be satisfied by an implementer who writes the pin and its render half as two tests, which the house style invites.

The proposal also wrote its browser half by booting the app and driving headless Chromium over raw CDP, and its figures reproduce the reviewer's and QA's independent measurements to the digit. I did not re-measure them; I took them as one agent's execution and say so in confidence_rationale and residual_risks.
validated_work_order.root_cause:
Two independent causes, plus one pre-existing defect this ticket does not own.

(1) PRODUCT DEFECT, one declaration. src/web/styles.css scopes overflow-wrap: anywhere to four card classes (.experiment-card, .opportunity-row, .approval-card, .learning-card) at styles.css:394-399. .awaiting-list is display: grid (styles.css:455) and .awaiting-list li (styles.css:463) carries no overflow-wrap, so the li is a grid item floored at its content's min-content width, and one long unbreakable decision_id — the same free text the four named lists already wrap — sizes the whole track. The rendered markup is pages.js:695-697, a <ul class="awaiting-list"> whose <strong> holds the decision_id. A grid item's automatic minimum is the token's min-content width, which is exactly what overflow-wrap: anywhere removes and break-word does not. Two independent measurements agree on the mechanism at different fixture lengths (the review's 1672px at 140 characters, QA's 1443px at 120).

(2) TEST-INFRASTRUCTURE DEFECT, one missing abstraction, in EIGHT places not five. test/web/pages.test.js reads src/web/styles.css at lines 345, 359, 1633, 1653, 1693, 1757, 1802 and 1819 and builds its own regex for selectors, bodies or declarations at each. The card pin at 1693 had to grow three defensive layers — comment stripping, exact-compound selector matching, a scoped later-override check — because its parse was the weakest; the other seven re-derive weaker versions of those same three things from raw text. Review findings 1, 3, 4 and 5 are four specific ways one of those weaker parses returns a false green, and all four plus two more the ticket never names reproduce against the exact current regexes.

(3) PRE-EXISTING, different mechanism, diagnosed here and not fixed here: /approvals at a 320px viewport reads documentElement.scrollWidth 309 against clientWidth 305 on clean main, from three li.approval-card at right edge 309. li.approval-card computes min-width: auto and is a grid item of ul.approval-list (styles.css:367-372, display: grid) whose resolved track is 268px inside a 223px box; .approval-card (styles.css:376-381) is itself display: grid and declares no min-width, so its automatic minimum is its min-content width and that is what floors the track. The critic measured min-width: 0 injected on .approval-card taking scrollWidth 309 -> 305 and the offender count 3 -> 0. It is recorded in AC-10 as a named pre-existing offender so a sweep can tell it from a regression.
validated_work_order.approach:
Three changes, one per root cause, plus one test I am adding as arbiter. 'The shared reader' below means the same three helpers and one contract test, and every stylesheet pin in the file ends up using them — there is no second parser left at the end of this change.

A. Add `overflow-wrap: anywhere;` to the EXISTING `.awaiting-list li` rule in src/web/styles.css, in place alongside its display/gap/border/radius/padding declarations — not as a second rule with the same selector, which would make the fix's own duplicate selector read as an override of itself to the very check this change adds. One declaration plus a comment in the same voice and for the same reason as the existing wrap rule at styles.css:385: a grid item is floored at its min-content width, the decision_id is free text, `anywhere` rather than `break-word` because break-word leaves intrinsic sizing alone. Then pin it in the house style, with a render half so it is a fact about the page and not about the file: /journal at override 'partial' against the seeded repositories must emit class="awaiting-list" and an <li data-decision-id=...> whose <strong> holds the decision_id. dec_seed_awaiting_1 renders inside that list from the existing seed, so no new fixture is needed. Do NOT fold .awaiting-list li into the four-class card rule: that rule's assertion requires exactly those four bare selectors, and a descendant selector on a different structural shape would satisfy a selector the pages never render as a bare class.

B. Add three shared helpers near the top of test/web/pages.test.js, beside the existing H1_HOOK and mainOf helpers, each with a comment naming what it defends against, and route ALL EIGHT stylesheet tests through them. Keep every existing assertion and every existing failure message verbatim; only the plumbing moves.

  `cssRules(source)` strips /* */ comments first, then walks the source with a brace stack. A rule inside an at-rule is emitted with its OWN selector and a `nested: true` flag, so `@media (max-width: 900px) { .approval-card { overflow-wrap: normal } }` is a rule whose selector is `.approval-card`, not one whose selector is the at-rule prelude. The current /([^{}]+)\{([^}]*)\}/g captures that media block as one rule whose selector is the at-rule prelude and whose body is literal text, which is exactly why the card pin's override filter finds no card class and passes. Every rule carries a source `index`. The prototype the proposal ran against the real stylesheet emits 68 rules in source order, with eight nested: #main:focus, .skeleton, #journal-drawer, .journal-filters .journal-filter-control, .kpi-strip, #main, and the `0%` and `100%` step selectors @keyframes skeleton-pulse contributes. The keyframe steps are harmless because every lookup is an exact selector match, but say so in a comment: a later reader who finds them cold will reasonably assume they are a bug. Two implementation notes, both from running the prototype: ';' terminates a declaration inside a rule and a prelude inside an at-rule, and a frame whose selector starts with '@' is a block whose children are rules rather than a rule whose body is declarations. A version that appends nested text to the parent body silently drops every nested rule and reintroduces review finding 3 exactly, while still passing every test in the file as written today. The reader must not emit at-rule frames themselves, or the forced-colors block comes back as one rule named `@media (forced-colors: active)`.

  `declarations(body, prop)` returns one property's values from an already comment-stripped body, anchored on a declaration boundary (start of body or after a ';') rather than a bare substring, or `min-width` also matches inside a longer property name. Split the body on ';' and treat a trailing non-empty chunk as a declaration, or normalise the body to end in ';' — CSS does not require a final semicolon, every shipped body here happens to have one, and the two bodies where that matters most are the ones whose only declaration is last: `.page-title`'s `line-height: 1.25` and `#main > *`'s `min-width: 0`. Without this, a formatter or a hand edit that drops one semicolon removes a declaration from a pin whose whole job is noticing deleted declarations, and nothing on the shipped file surfaces it. This is the fix for review findings 4 and 5: the min-width pin runs /min-width\s*:\s*([^;]+);/ over the RAW body, so a rule with no min-width at all but a comment naming one reads as ['16ch'], count 1, green — the BUG-1 state passing the BUG-1 pin — and a comment beside a real declaration is consumed as the declaration.

  `conflictingOverrides(rules, rule, selectors, prop)` replaces what the proposal called laterOverrides, and the signature change is the most important correction in this order. The card pin's current loop walks only rules that pass `.filter((rule) => /overflow-wrap\s*:/.test(rule.body))` at pages.test.js:1699, and that property filter is load-bearing: it is what makes the comment's promise true, that a rule which cannot override the card classes does not turn the suite red. A helper taking only a selector set either drops that filter — in which case the first `@media (max-width: 900px) { .awaiting-list li { padding: var(--space-3) } }` narrow-viewport tweak, a shape this stylesheet already contains twice at 497 and 508, turns the new pin red for a declaration that cannot change overflow-wrap — or hardcodes overflow-wrap inside, in which case the seven non-wrap pins gain a check that can never fire and AC-7's stated mutation is not caught. Take the property as a fourth argument and filter inside on `declarations(other.body, prop).length > 0`. Report a conflict for ANY rule other than the pinned one, at ANY source index, top-level or nested, that declares `prop` on a comma-part of its selector equal to a member of `selectors` — symmetric in source order, because an override authored ABOVE the pinned rule wins at narrow viewports exactly as one below does, and the shipped forced-colors carve-out is the one existing case of that shape. Today this is free: the stylesheet declares each pinned property once per selector, and no at-rule in the file names a pinned selector. Call it from each pin with its own selector set and its own property. The one exclusion: `#main:focus`, whose one later same-selector rule is the intentional @media (forced-colors: active) carve-out, already pinned by AC-8 — adding the check there blind would fail the file on the shipped stylesheet.

  CRITICAL, and it is the highest-leverage line in the change: the selector lookup must anchor on the SELECTOR'S END — match a comma-split part with `===` against the pinned selector, never `selector.includes(pinnedSelector)`. '.opportunity-roww' and '.tenant-names' both contain their pinned selector as a substring, and a substring lookup silently deletes the rename protection the current `\s*\{` anchors give every pin in the file, one bug across eight pins, invisible because nothing else in the suite catches a rename.

  THE FORCED-COLORS PIN IS THE ONE THAT NEEDS CARE, NOT A MECHANICAL SWAP, and this order makes a deliberate decision the critique asked to see made. The current regex at pages.test.js:360 is /@media\s*\(forced-colors:\s*active\)\s*\{[^@]*?#main:focus\s*\{([^}]*)\}/, and its `[^@]*?` means it only finds the carve-out when the carve-out is the first thing in the block. The shared reader finds it wherever it sits, so the rewrite is strictly MORE PERMISSIVE. That loosening is accepted, on purpose, and pinned: the assertions that carry the meaning — the carve-out exists, declares `outline: 2px solid CanvasText`, and is declared AFTER the bare #main:focus rule at equal specificity, because both selectors are 1,1,0 — are unchanged, and a mutation that puts another nested rule before the carve-out must still pass so the loosening is a stated behaviour rather than a silent one. State in the test's comment why it was rewritten: the parser's strictness changed, not the assertion. Note also that the ordering comparison does not need the reader: `css.search(/#main:focus\s*\{/)` already gives the bare rule's offset today, so the real reason to rewrite this test is that its body parse cannot see the block at all.

  ONE TEST I AM ADDING AS ARBITER, which neither document asked for: a contract test for the three helpers, driven by fixture strings rather than by the shipped stylesheet, asserting what the eight pins now depend on — a comment-only min-width reads as no declarations, an at-rule-nested rule carries its own selector, a later same-selector rule declaring an UNRELATED property is not a conflict, a media-nested overflow-wrap override IS a conflict, an override authored ABOVE the pinned rule is a conflict, and a renamed class does not match. The eight-pin migration currently has no automated guard on the plumbing at all: every proof it works is a mutation a reviewer has to run by hand, and the helpers will outlive this ticket. It is ~30 lines, adds one test to the file, and is the one addition here a maintainer can drop without touching the fix. If you drop it, the qa_script mutation matrix becomes the helpers' only proof and residual_risks says so.

C. Fix the pre-existing red test, because nothing else in this change is verifiable while it is red — AC-3 and AC-5 both read the file's totals, and a red file makes every count in this order ambiguous. The assertion is /<li class="approval-card">/ and the markup is `<li class="approval-card" data-testid="approval-card" data-approval-card ...>`: a qa/selectors.md-stable data-testid was added to the element after the matcher was written, and the matcher anchors on the closing '>'. The fix is /<li class="approval-card"[\s>]/. `\b` does not work and the reason is worth a comment: after the closing quote both the quote and the following space are non-word characters, so there is no boundary there. While in that helper, drop the `approval.requested` raw-event append from pendingApprovalRepos — grep finds exactly two hits in the whole repository, the helper's own docstring and the append — and rewrite the docstring to say what is actually true: the approval cards come from the seed's three SEEDED_PENDING_IDS (apv_seed_budget_1, apv_seed_campaign_1, apv_seed_geography_1, written through the approvals repository at scripts/seed.js:579), not from a raw event, and no test in this file renders an approval card without that seed. The existing docstring's cited evidence is wrong as well as stale: it points at 'the read at src/web/pages.js:924' and that line is experiment-card markup. Do not write 'four pending' anywhere — three pending, four seeded, one lapsed.

A whole-body assertion would also force the fix into a SECOND `.awaiting-list li` rule, whose duplicate selector the conflict check would then read as an override of itself — the fix breaking its own guard.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep the forced-colors pin as strict as it is: assert the carve-out is the first rule inside the @media (forced-colors: active) block, as the `[^@]*?` regex effectively does today.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The strictness was an accident of the regex, not the property under test. What the test is about is that a carve-out exists, declares the system colour, and comes after the bare rule at equal specificity; 'first in the block' is none of those. The loosening is accepted, stated in the rewritten test's comment, and pinned by a green case so a future reader meets it as a decision rather than as a difference.

alternatives_considered.approach: Land the forced-colors source-order mutation as a test that feeds a reordered stylesheet string through the helpers, instead of leaving it to the qa_script.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: This is the critique's suggestion in its strongest form, and it is right about the gap. It is declined in that exact form only because the helper contract test (AC-11) already covers the reader's behaviour on fixture strings, including above-the-rule overrides, and adding a second fixture-driven test would be a third copy of the same idea. The specific mutation — move the carve-out above the bare rule — is kept in tests[] and the qa_script because it proves the PINS react, which the helper test cannot do, and because it is a one-line edit a reviewer can apply in seconds.

alternatives_considered.approach: Have the new awaiting-list render half create its own awaiting decision through the repository instead of relying on the seed's dec_seed_awaiting_1.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: A real fragility, but the same one every existing render half in this file carries — the card pin already depends on the seed rendering the pending approvals. Both paths are constructible, so the choice is convention. I kept seededRepos and recorded the dependency in residual_risks rather than adding a fixture only this test uses.

assumptions: The `ch` unit is the correct unit for the pin's stated property, resting on `ch` being the advance width of '0' in the element's font. This was not verified to hold for every glyph in the reason field — a reason is typed text, not zeroes, and the two differ in width. The 59px-versus-162.9px contrast that motivates the pin is measured; the 'twelve characters' phrasing is the pin's own and is kept rather than restated in a unit that cannot be measured per-glyph.

Narrowing the min-width regex to ch-only does not block a legitimate future edit. I judged a px floor a restatement in ch rather than a loss, but that is a judgement about this repo's habit, not something the code or the docs settle.

Migrating all eight pins rather than five is the right scope. The ticket's own subject is the class of false green, and a shared reader applied to five of eight sites leaves the class open in three places, two of which were reproduced going green with their declaration deleted.

The pre-existing red test is a stale matcher and not a deliberate pin. The evidence is that the element carries a qa/selectors.md-stable data-testid the matcher cannot see, and that the file goes 72/72 when the matcher is corrected. No commit that deliberately narrowed it was found.

A property-filtered override check is the right contract for all eight migrated pins, including the ones that are not wrap pins. The alternative — one helper per property — is more general and is finding 6's shape again.

The new .awaiting-list li pin asserting the property per-rule is the right strictness, following the #main > * and .tenant-name pins rather than the card and drawer pins' whole-body form. If the house style is tightening toward whole-body, this pin is looser than it needs to be.
unknowns: Whether a decision_id in a real deployment can reach 120+ unbreakable characters. The repository accepts any string and the API auto-creates tenants from free-text request headers, so a long id is constructible; whether it occurs in practice is a production question. The defect is real and reachable either way and its severity is unchanged by how often it fires — the same argument the QA report made in rating the finding minor.

Whether 1ch = 10.18px holds on the platforms this app actually runs on. It is a property of the resolved system-ui font and will differ on macOS and Windows. This is precisely why the pin does not hard-code a ratio — but it does mean the twelve-character threshold is font-relative by construction, and anyone revisiting the floor should measure rather than assume.

Whether the browser figures (1672, 1629, 221/276/315, 305/360/399, the six-route sweep, the 4px, 1ch = 10.18px) match a headed browser rather than headless Chromium on this runner. The proposal measured them over raw CDP because the repo has no browser driver and its dependencies are express only; I did not re-measure any of them. Font rasterization and scrollbar metrics can differ, though the layout mechanism — a grid item floored at its min-content width — is not browser-specific. Two independent sources agree on that mechanism at different fixture lengths, which is the load-bearing part.

Whether the shared reader behaves as the prototype did on the real stylesheet. The proposal reports 68 rules in source order with all eleven pinned selectors resolving and the forced-colors pairing at indices 14 and 15; I did not run the prototype. The AC-11 contract test is what makes the reader's behaviour a checked fact rather than a claim, and it is why I would not drop it.

Whether anything outside this repository reads the `approval.requested` raw event the test helper appends. Within src/, test/ and scripts/ nothing does — the only two hits are the helper's own docstring and the append — and /approvals renders three cards with and without it. If an external consumer exists, removing the append from a test fixture is still correct, but it cannot be seen from inside the tree.
validated_work_order.confidence_rationale: Everything structural in this order I checked against the current tree myself rather than taking either document's word: the eight stylesheet read sites and their line numbers, the card pin's property filter at pages.test.js:1699 (which is what the corrected helper signature is built around), the current min-width regex /^(ch|rem|px)$/ and its bare-number comparison, the comment-blind regexes in the #main:focus, .page-title and min-width pins, the .approval-list / .approval-card / .experiment-card grid rules that floor the /approvals track, the forced-colors block containing nothing but the carve-out, the awaiting-list markup at pages.js:695-697, the stale docstring's cited line (pages.js:924 is experiment-card markup) and the baseline itself — `node --test test/web/pages.test.js` reads 72/71/1 on this tree, which is what AC-3 and AC-5 are calibrated against. What holds this at 85 rather than lower is that the load-bearing claims have been measured by someone, twice, independently: the two browser measurements of the wrap defect agree to the digit at different fixture lengths, and the v1 rejection's own arithmetic is confirmed by both agents running the pair in a real browser. It is not 90 for three reasons, all of them real. I did not re-measure a single browser figure myself, and the reader prototype is the proposal's execution rather than mine. I changed the helper's contract and two acceptance thresholds after the fact, so more of this order than either document's is unexecuted — the directions are checked against the code, the exact behaviour is not. And the ch-only narrowing remains a judgement about a test's strictness rather than a verified defect, which the proposer flagged as its own top risk and I have upheld. Moving up would need a headed-browser confirmation of the three widths and one run of the reader prototype against the real stylesheet; moving down would need a reason to think the seed's awaiting decision or the exact-selector anchoring is less stable than measured, or that the four named pre-existing offenders on /approvals are something else.
evidence: the eight read sites: grep for styles.css in test/web/pages.test.js returns 8 hits at lines 345, 359, 1633, 1653, 1693, 1757, 1802 and 1819. the card pin's override loop is property-filtered today (mine, read at pages.test.js:1697-1699): `.filter((rule) => /overflow-wrap\s*:/.test(rule.body))` before the loop at :1716. This is why the corrected helper takes the property as an argument rather than inferring it, and it is the single most consequential correction this order makes to the proposal.

min-width unit false green (review finding 1), confirmed by reading the shipped regex: the pin at pages.test.js:1771 is /^(\d+(?:\.\d+)?)(ch|rem|px)$/ with the assertion Number(floor[1]) >= 12. `min-width: 12px` therefore matches with floor[1] === '12' and passes — the pin is green on the defect it was written to replace. `min-width: 1rem` and `min-width: 8ch` are red today because 1 >= 12 and 8 >= 12 are both false, which is why they prove the rule rather than the fix. `min-width: 16CH` is red today because the regex is case-sensitive.

at-rule blind spot (review finding 3): the card pin's /([^{}]+)\{([^}]*)\}/g pattern captures an appended `@media (max-width: 900px) { .approval-card { overflow-wrap: normal; } }` as ONE rule whose selector is the at-rule prelude and whose body is literal text, so the selector filter finds no card class and the loop passes. comment blindness in three pins, confirmed by reading each regex (mine): /#main:focus\s*\{([^}]*)\}/ at :346 and /\.page-title\s*\{([^}]*)\}/ at :1634 run over the raw file, and the min-width pin at :1766-1769 runs /min-width\s*:\s*([^;]+);/g over the raw body. The min-width case is the sharpest: a rule with no min-width at all but a comment naming 16ch reads as ['16ch'], count 1, which is the BUG-1 state passing the BUG-1 pin.

seed split, confirmed by me in scripts/seed.js: SEEDED_PENDING_IDS holds 3 entries (apv_seed_budget_1, apv_seed_campaign_1, apv_seed_geography_1) and SEEDED_APPROVAL_IDS holds 4 including SEEDED_LAPSED_ID. The critique rendered /approvals with and without the raw-event append and got 3 cards, 3 forms, 3 reason inputs and 2 buttons either way, so dropping the append satisfies both callers at :1731 and :1778.

the calibration strings, measured by the critique on a seeded database: 'Precision 1.00 over 2 matured decisions', 'False-intervention rate 0.00 over 1 interventions', '2 awaiting maturity', longest whitespace-delimited token 18 characters ('False-intervention'). sibling surfaces, swept by the critique: the only other display:grid lists are .experiment-list/.experiment-card and .approval-list/.approval-card (both carrying overflow-wrap but neither carrying min-width: 0 — the approval one is the 4px), .checklist/.checklist li (hardcoded strings, cannot be floored by free text), .kpi-strip/.kpi-card (money and counts, longest token well under 305px) and .learning-list/.learning-card (wrapped). `.awaiting-list li` is the only unwrapped free-text surface.
residual_risks: Every browser figure in this order comes from headless Chromium driven over raw CDP, because the repo has no browser driver and its dependencies are express only. I did not re-measure any of them. Font rasterization and scrollbar metrics can differ from a headed browser, though the layout mechanism — a grid item floored at its min-content width — is not browser-specific. QA should confirm against a real browser rather than take these numbers as the acceptance, and should read them against the 15px scrollbar note in qa_script step 4 rather than the literal numbers.

The helpers carry the whole automated half of this ticket and the only automated coverage of a layout defect. AC-11 pins their contract on fixture strings, but a fixture test only pins the cases someone thought of: a selector list with a comma inside a functional pseudo-class, a nested at-rule inside a nested at-rule, a declaration with a value containing a semicolon inside quotes or a url(), and an @supports block are all unhandled by anything in this order.

The override check is a same-selector-set check, so a higher-specificity override on a different selector — `.awaiting-list > li`, `#journal-drawer .awaiting-list li`, or a `.panel .awaiting-list li` — reinstates the page overflow with a green suite. The `.awaiting-list li strong` and `li span` cases are covered because the fix works by inheritance onto them and they are the plausible edit; a descendant or id-qualified rewrite of the same rule is not. QA should go there first.

The override check is directional in one respect that could not be closed cheaply: an at-rule block authored ABOVE the pinned rule is caught, but only because the check now reports conflicts at any index. What it cannot see is specificity — a rule with higher specificity declaring the same property later still wins in the browser and is not reported if its selector text differs. That is the residual behind the bullet above and is a property of the check, not a bug in it.

The new tests' render halves depend on the seed still containing an awaiting-maturity decision (dec_seed_awaiting_1) and the three pending approvals. That is the same seed dependency every existing render half in this file carries, so it is house convention rather than a new hazard, but a future seed cleanup would turn these pins red for a reason unrelated to the CSS.

The narrow-viewport sweep runs headless with no forced-colors emulation. A forced-colors browser check was judged unnecessary — forced-colors forces colour and contrast, and does not alter overflow-wrap or intrinsic sizing, so a wrap that applies in the default mode applies there too — but that is reasoning, not a measurement, and the stylesheet does carry a forced-colors carve-out for #main:focus.

The ch-only narrowing is a strictness decision with no pin on the pin. Whoever hits a legitimate `min-width: 96px` first has a cheaper fix available than restating it in ch, and that cheaper fix re-admits `min-width: 12px` — the exact value this ticket exists to close. A maintainer should decide this deliberately rather than let the first person to trip it decide.
validated_work_order.debate_summary:
The critique's verdict on the diagnosis was 'flawed' with a root-cause verdict of 'RIGHT', and I agree with both halves: nothing below attacks the premise, and I re-checked the load-bearing claims myself rather than taking either document's word. Four of its findings changed this order, two majors and two minors, and one of the four is the single most consequential line in it.

The one that matters most is the helper signature, and I want to be plain that the proposal got it wrong. It proposed `laterOverrides(rules, rule, selectors)` and asked each pin to call it with its own selector set. The card pin's existing loop filters candidate rules on `/overflow-wrap\s*:/` at pages.test.js:1699 before walking them, and that filter is what makes the comment above it true — that a rule which cannot override the card classes does not turn the suite red. Take the property away and you get one of two failures: drop the filter, and the first `@media (max-width: 900px) { .awaiting-list li { padding: var(--space-3) } }` narrow-viewport tweak — a shape this stylesheet already contains twice, at 497 and 508 — turns the new pin red for a declaration that cannot change overflow-wrap, which is finding 6 recurring one ticket after the ticket that closed it; or hardcode overflow-wrap inside the helper, and the seven non-wrap pins get a check that can never fire and AC-7's stated mutation goes uncatchable. I took the property as a fourth argument. I also made the check symmetric in source order, because the critique's own missed-edge-case list names an override authored ABOVE the rule, and the one existing case of that shape in this stylesheet is the forced-colors carve-out — so a later-only check is a check that will be wrong the first time somebody puts a narrow-viewport block at the top of the file.

AC-10's threshold is the second correction, and I disagreed with the proposal here for a reason the critique had already measured. The proposal kept `right > window.innerWidth` and defended it by recording the pre-change baseline per route, on the grounds that /approvals carries a pre-existing 4px so a clientWidth sweep would fail a correct implementation. The baseline recording is right and I kept it. The threshold is still wrong: window.innerWidth includes the 15px classic scrollbar and clientWidth does not, so the check cannot see any overflow narrower than a scrollbar, and the proposal's own 4px is the demonstration — invisible at innerWidth, visible at clientWidth, same page. The critique dissolves the dilemma rather than choosing in it: sweep at clientWidth and tell the known offenders apart by name, which is what AC-10 now does. I also upheld the sub-point that the same threshold had leaked into qa_script step 6, so a reviewer following the script would have inherited the blind spot without knowing it.

The third correction is AC-5, and it is smaller but it would have cost a run. The proposal pinned exact totals — 73/73 in the file, 472/472 across the suite — while its own tests[] enumerated the new pin's render half as a separate case, which reads as a second test and is idiomatic in this file. An implementer who writes two tests produces 74/74 and 473/473, is entirely correct, and fails the criterion with no way to see why. I restated it as a delta plus a test name and gave the figures conditionally, and the same reasoning is why I added the second test the order now specifies: with the file at 74 the exact numbers are no longer worth pinning at all.

The fourth is minor and cheap: `declarations()` must treat a trailing chunk after the last ';' as a declaration. CSS does not require a final semicolon, every shipped body in this stylesheet happens to have one, and the two bodies where it matters most are the ones whose only declaration is last — `.page-title`'s `line-height: 1.25` and `#main > *`'s `min-width: 0`. The proposal's own verification could not surface this, which is exactly why it would have been found later.

What I took from the minors besides that: AC-1 and AC-2 are restated so they cannot be satisfied by an empty render — the panel is reachable only through a preview override, so 'every li computes overflow-wrap: anywhere' and 'scrollWidth 305' are both satisfied by a page that rendered the wrong shell, which is the default failure mode for a reviewer on this route. The pin watches `.awaiting-list li strong` and `li span` for overrides, because the fix works by inheritance onto those grid items and a later rule on the strong reinstates the defect with a green suite. The pendingApprovalRepos docstring is now specified rather than merely 'rewritten', because the existing one is the only statement of why an approval card renders in that fixture at all: the new text names the seed's three SEEDED_PENDING_IDS as the real supplier, which is strictly more accurate than what it replaces. And the forced-colors rewrite is a deliberate, stated, pinned loosening rather than an accident — the old `[^@]*?` only found the carve-out as the first rule in its block, and the new reader finds it anywhere, so I made the looser case a required green mutation and said in the test's comment why it changed. The critique asked for a decision between keeping the old strictness and accepting the loosening; I took the loosening, because 'first in the block' was a property of the regex and not of the thing under test, which is that a carve-out exists, declares the system colour, and comes after the bare rule at equal specificity.

What I dismissed, and why. The critique's first option on the /approvals 4px was to fix it here — one declaration, `min-width: 0` on `.approval-card`, measured to take scrollWidth 309 to 305. I confirmed the mechanism myself from the stylesheet: ul.approval-list is display: grid, li.approval-card is a grid item whose own rule is display: grid with no min-width, so its automatic minimum is its min-content width, and `#main > *` lifts the floor for main's direct children but not for the li inside the list. The critique is right and its measurement stands. I did not take the fix, and this is the one place I knowingly left a real, one-line defect on the table. It is a different mechanism from both defects this ticket owns, on a surface none of the eight findings names, and it would be an unrequested edit to a rule shared with .experiment-card; taking it would also mean the browser half of this ticket depends on a fix nobody asked for. I took the critique's stated alternative instead — keep it out of scope, replace the proposal's 'I am not going to guess' with the actual diagnosis, and name its three offenders in AC-10 so the sweep is strict everywhere else — and recorded the exact declaration in out_of_scope so the follow-up is one line. If a maintainer would rather absorb it here, that is a one-declaration change to the stylesheet entry and nothing else in this order needs to move.

I also declined the critique's stronger suggestion on the forced-colors mutation: land it as a test that feeds a reordered stylesheet string through the helpers rather than leaving it to a reviewer to run by hand. The critique is right that the eight-pin migration currently has no automated guard on its own plumbing. I got most of that another way — the helper contract test in files[] item (5), driven by fixture strings, which is my addition and which neither document asked for. Between the two I have one fixture-driven test rather than two, and the specific mutation stays in the qa_script because it proves the PINS react, which a helper test cannot do. That test is also why the reader prototype's behaviour stops being a claim: AC-11 makes it a checked fact. It is separable, it is ~30 lines, and a maintainer who wants the order smaller can drop it and lose only AC-11.

Where I differ from both documents: I did not re-measure a single browser figure. I read the CSS, I read the pins, and I ran the baseline myself, but 1672, 1629, 221/276/315, 305/360/399, the six-route sweep, the 4px and 1ch = 10.18px are two agents' executions that I am relaying, not mine. That, plus the fact that I changed the helper's contract and two thresholds after the fact so that more of this order is unexecuted than either document's, is most of why this is an 85 and not the proposal's 90. The other reason is the ch-only narrowing, which is a judgement about a test's strictness rather than a verified defect and which I have upheld: accepting px is exactly how `min-width: 12px`, the original defect, stays green, and a runner-specific px-to-ch ratio would be green here and wrong on another platform's system-ui. It is one decision, isolated in one regex, and cheap to overrule.
